title: 10ish Worst Business Decisions Ever
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck cover a handful of famous business blunders instead of a full top-ten list: Alexander Graham Bell and Western Union, Excite passing on Google, Kodak missing digital photography, JCPenney's fair-and-square pricing under Ron Johnson, New Coke, Blockbuster passing on Netflix, the ET/Reese's Pieces product placement decision, and ABC's gamble on Monday Night Football. Includes a brief listener mail segment about sailing and a plug for a Dave Ruse-written article.
topics: Alexander Graham Bell telephone Western Union
JCPenney Ron Johnson fair and square pricing

segments.title: Opening and concept
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode as a series of bad business decisions rather than a full top-ten list, noting they picked eight entries in advance.

segments.title: Alexander Graham Bell and Western Union
segments.summary: Bell offered his telephone patent to Western Union for one hundred thousand dollars, and they declined. Bell instead founded his own company. The hosts note Bell originally envisioned the telephone as a broadcast device for performances rather than two-way talk.

segments.title: Excite passes on buying Google
segments.summary: Excite, a web portal, reportedly turned down buying Google for a million dollars and then for seven hundred and fifty thousand dollars in 1999. Two competing accounts are given: Excite's CEO George Bell said the deal would have harmed their engineering team, while Google's side said Excite's search test results were too good to give up.

segments.title: Kodak and digital photography
segments.summary: Kodak engineer Steve Sasson built an early digital camera in the mid-1970s, but company leadership resisted it. Kodak spent billions on digital efforts but was passed by competitors, laid off many workers, and filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 2012.

segments.title: JCPenney and Ron Johnson's fair and square pricing
segments.summary: CEO Ron Johnson, former Target and Apple retail executive, ended JCPenney's sale-and-coupon pricing in favor of everyday low prices called fair and square. Customers reacted badly, sales dropped sharply, and he was out after about seventeen months, with the company returning to sales-based pricing.

segments.title: New Coke
segments.summary: Coca-Cola reformulated its drink in 1985 partly in response to Pepsi's gains, and New Coke was a flop. Coca-Cola Classic returned within about three months. The hosts discuss taste tests and the psychology of changing a beloved product.

segments.title: Blockbuster passes on Netflix
segments.summary: Blockbuster reportedly turned down Netflix's offer to merge or be acquired for about fifty million dollars, and later copied the DVD mailing model. Netflix later shut down its DVD service, and Blockbuster went bankrupt in 2010 and was bought by Dish.

segments.title: Blockbuster's later decisions and Netflix stock swings
segments.summary: Hosts describe Blockbuster's later CEOs spending money on failed schemes instead of returning cash to shareholders. They also discuss Netflix's stock volatility and its DVD shutdown, with the company giving away leftover discs.

segments.title: E.T. and Reese's Pieces product placement
segments.summary: Mars reportedly declined to spend a million dollars on a promotion tie-in with E.T., so Hershey's Reese's Pieces took the deal, which is credited with boosting the candy. Accounts differ on who championed the idea, including Steven Spielberg, Steve Adler at MCA, and business development VP Jack Dowd. The hosts also note E.T. is among the highest-grossing non-franchise films.

segments.title: Monday Night Football origins
segments.summary: The NFL struggled to find a network for prime-time games. CBS and NBC declined, and ABC took the gamble, starting Monday Night Football in 1970 with a Browns-Jets game, anchored by Keith Jackson, Frank Gifford, Don Meredith, and Howard Cosell. The hosts note Joe Namath's role in choosing the Jets.

segments.title: Football history tangent and Reese's Pieces debate
segments.summary: Hosts discuss Cosell's broadcasting style and the longevity of Monday Night Football, then debate whether Reese's Pieces contain chocolate. The hosts agree they are a candy-coated peanut butter confection.

segments.title: Listener mail on sailing
segments.summary: A listener named Sam suggests an episode on sailing and the hosts respond, noting the wind pushing and pulling a boat. Listeners can email Stuff Podcasts at iHeartRadio dot com with topic suggestions.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing credits noting the show is a production of iHeartRadio.
